Sheepcote
shēp´kōt
n. (an enclosure for sheep; the place David was taken from)
From sheep + cote, a small shelter or hut (Old English cote, a cottage). The KJV uses it for the rough field enclosure — a wall of stones, sometimes a cave — where a flock was penned at night.

Biblical Definition

Israel's greatest king is repeatedly identified by the place he was fetched from, and it was not a palace or a school. “He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds” (Psalm 78:70), and the next verse keeps the smell of the work in it: “From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance” (Psalm 78:71). The verb in both lines is God's — He chose, He took, He brought — and the training given was the care of pregnant ewes, which is to say the care of the weak and the slow, the exact skill a shepherd of Israel would need. The day of his anointing shows how little anyone else valued the post: “And Samuel said unto Jesse, Are here all thy children? And he said, There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep. And Samuel said unto Jesse, Send and fetch him: for we will not sit down till he come hither” (1 Samuel 16:11). His own father did not think to call him in. Later the sheepcote appears again as the setting of David's severest test: “And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where was a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet: and David and his men remained in the sides of the cave” (1 Samuel 24:3) — where the shepherd spared the king who hunted him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a sheepcote as a small enclosure for sheep; a pen — from cote, a cottage, hut, or shed.

expand to see more

SHEEPCOTE, n. A small inclosure for sheep; a pen.

COTE, n. A cot; a hut; a sheep-fold.

SHEEPFOLD, n. A place where sheep are collected or confined.

EWE, n. A female sheep; the female of the ovine race of animals.

SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the pasture. In Scripture, one who exercises pastoral care over a flock.

Key Scripture

Psalm 78:70 — "He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds:"

Psalm 78:71 — "From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance."

1 Samuel 16:11 — "And Samuel said unto Jesse, Are here all thy children? And he said, There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep. And Samuel said unto Jesse, Send and fetch him: for we will not sit down till he come hither."

1 Samuel 24:3 — "And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where was a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet: and David and his men remained in the sides of the cave."

Modern Corruption

The shepherd image is sentimentalized into gentleness, and the sheepcote — a hard, dirty, dangerous post — disappears from the picture of what pastoral care actually costs.

expand to see more

Every church window with a smiling shepherd and a clean lamb works against Psalm 78:71. The training was following ewes great with young — slow, filthy, night work in lambing season, at the mercy of weather and predators, for animals that cannot be reasoned with. That is what God chose as the apprenticeship for a king, and the New Testament keeps the word for elders. A man who wants the title of pastor and not the sheepcote has mistaken the office for a platform.

The second thing the sentimental picture loses is the sheepcote's danger to the shepherd himself. 1 Samuel 24 puts David in one, with Saul unarmed and asleep at the mouth of the cave, and his own men quoting providence at him to justify the kill. He cut a hem and his heart smote him. The sheepfold is where a man finds out whether he will take by force what God has already promised to give, and that test comes to anyone who has been anointed for something and made to wait for it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gederah (H1448), a wall, sheepfold; mikla (H4356), a fold, pen; ul (H5763), ewes giving suck; roeh (H7462), a shepherd.

expand to see more

Hebrew gederah (H1448) — a stone wall, enclosure; the sheepcotes of 1 Samuel 24:3.

Hebrew mikla (H4356) — a fold, pen; the sheepfolds of Psalm 78:70.

Hebrew alah (H5763) — giving suck, great with young; the ewes David followed.

Hebrew raah (H7462) — to feed, tend, shepherd; used of David and of the LORD, Psalm 23:1.

Greek poimaino (G4165) — to shepherd, tend; the charge given to Peter, John 21:16.

Usage

"“Took him from the sheepfolds” — God's verbs throughout."

"“Following the ewes great with young” — the apprenticeship for a throne."

"“There remaineth yet the youngest” — his own father did not send for him."
